Problem 59: When the statement and working disagree

The literal edition states height 12 and base side 8, then works with 8 to make 6. Read both sets of dimensions.

Selected step 4: Notice the second discrepancy. Selected dimensions: used in the working (side 12, height 8).

A modern section at equal scales: base 12, height 8. The horizontal measure is 5 1/4 palms per vertical cubit. One cubit is seven palms; one palm is four fingers.

Chace’s literal edition retains a result of five palms and two fingers and marks “2” as a mistake for “1.” Peet’s translation prints the corrected one finger. Neither result agrees with height 12 and base side 8 as written.

  1. Keep the written statement visible

    Height 12 and base side 8 give a half-base of 4. That triangle has a seked of 2 1/3 palms. Use the reading switch to compare it with the dimensions implied by the working.

    as written: 7 × 4/12 = 7/3 palms

  2. Read what the arithmetic actually does

    The working asks for the fraction of 8 that makes 6. A half and a quarter do that. This matches a height of 8 and a base side of 12, reversing the stated dimensions.

    8 × (1/2 + 1/4) = 6

  3. Convert the worked fraction

    Multiplying three quarters by seven gives 5 1/4 palms: five palms and one finger. The unit-fraction rows support this number.

    7 × (1/2 + 1/4) = 21/4 palms

  4. Notice the second discrepancy

    The literal edition prints five palms and two fingers, or 5 1/2 palms, and proposes one finger in a footnote. The working’s 5 1/4 and the printed result’s 5 1/2 stay separate here.

    worked: 21/4; printed result: 11/2 palms

  5. Compare the editions, not just the answers

    Peet prints the corrected five palms and one finger. Chace’s literal translation preserves two and footnotes the correction. The disagreement is visible in the included printed pages.

    statement ≠ working ≠ literal result

Selected reckoning rows

1/2 + 1/4: multiplier 3/4 × 8 = 6. Target 6. Target reached.

This table follows the arithmetic’s 8 and 6, even when the drawing is set to the written statement. Half plus quarter makes three quarters. The third and two-thirds rows are modern comparisons.

Words in the printed edition

mr · pyramid

The noun names the subject of problems 56–59B. The source drawing includes a low base line; the geometry in this app is a modern section.

mḥ · cubit

The arm measure appears when the calculation reduces the large triangle to a one-cubit rise. These exercises explicitly use a cubit of seven palms.

šsp · palm

Seven palms make the cubit used here. One finger is a quarter of a palm. The horizontal result can therefore be stated in palms and fingers.

iwn · pillar; a structure of uncertain form here

The word replaces “pyramid” in problem 60. A vocabulary gloss alone does not establish whether this particular figure is a cone, pyramid or another solid.

These are consonantal transliterations, not recovered pronunciations. The drawings are modern explanations; they do not reconstruct a named monument or its construction method. The face-slope interpretation follows the cited editions.

The complete source pages

Chace, Bull and Manning, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, volume II (1929). The transcription, literal translation and the two papyrus photographs are separate kinds of evidence. The plates reverse the transliteration’s letters and digits for right-to-left reading; the facing literal translation reads left to right. Peet’s 1923 p. 100 is also included for comparison.
